scope_note: Point B (post-implementation) audit of Task 5: server/internal/handler/access.go, routes.go, metrics.go, config.go, service/access.go, cmd/main.go, and the middleware.go wiring these files consume. Verified by full re-read of every listed file plus every neighboring file needed to reason about the trust boundary (http.go, auth.go, cors.go, all four new/changed test files), by running `go build ./...` and `go test ./...` (all green against live MariaDB), and by writing and executing two throwaway httptest probe files (not committed, removed after use) to empirically test the authorization-bypass and IDOR hypotheses called out in the brief rather than relying on static reading alone.

findings.title: /api/v1/users/** still trusts the URL path segment as the resource owner — any user with has_access=true can read/write/delete any other user's data
findings.description:
BuildRoutes correctly wraps /api/v1/users/ with RequireSameOrigin → RequireAuth → RequireAccess (Decision 6's gating half is done), but the handler behind it — APIHandler.handleUsers in server/internal/handler/http.go:27-38 — still takes `userID := parts[0]` straight from the URL path (`/api/v1/users/{userID}/...`), exactly as it did before this feature. RequireAccess only checks that the *caller* has has_access==true (or is admin); it never checks that the path's userID matches the caller's session identity. The result: any two ordinary, approved (has_access=true) users can act on each other's chats, settings, calculations and market-feedback simply by putting the other person's login in the path — full horizontal privilege escalation across every tenant's proprietary costing data.

Empirically confirmed with a throwaway httptest probe against the real BuildRoutes wiring (not a hypothetical): authenticated as `ivanov` (has_access=true), `POST /api/v1/users/petrov/chats` returned 201 and created a chat owned by `petrov`; `GET /api/v1/users/petrov/chats` then returned 200 with `petrov`'s chat list, including the newly created chat, entirely from `ivanov`'s session. The same path affects settings (GET/POST), chat deletion/restore, calculate, and market-feedback — i.e. every resource under this prefix.

This is not a Task-5 regression — Task 5's own scope note explicitly says the userID→session migration is Task 6's job, and tech-spec Decision 6 documents the same split. Task 6 is currently `status: planned` (not started). Flagging this regardless of planned sequencing: as of Task 5's completion, if this state were deployed to production, the vulnerability is live and trivially exploitable by any approved user (not just admins) — a single URL-segment change, no tooling required. The task's own acceptance criteria correctly scoped Task 5 to "gate by access" and left "gate by ownership" as a named follow-up, so this is a process/sequencing risk (don't ship between Task 5 and Task 6) rather than an implementation defect in the reviewed files — but it must be called out at full severity because the artifact, as it stands after Task 5, is exploitable.
findings.location: server/internal/handler/http.go:27-38 (handleUsers, userID from r.URL.Path) combined with server/internal/handler/routes.go:54-58 (RequireAccess gates access-level only, not resource ownership)
findings.impact: Any authenticated user who has been granted access (the normal, intended end state for most users, not a privileged group) can read, create, modify, and delete any other user's chats, calculations, and settings — a complete breach of tenant isolation for the product's core data. Also lets a low-privilege user drive up DeepSeek API spend via another user's market-feedback settings.
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy the access-control feature to production between Task 5 and Task 6 — or, if partial deploys are possible, land Task 6 (session-derived ownership for /api/v1/users/**) in the same release as Task 5, not as a separately shippable follow-up. As a stronger mitigation if these can't ship atomically: modify APIHandler.handleUsers to compare the path's userID against IdentityFromContext(r.Context()).Login and reject with 403 on mismatch until Task 6 replaces the path segment with the session-derived ID entirely.
findings.cwe: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

findings.title: SetAccess has a documented TOCTOU window between reading the access-request snapshot and deciding it
findings.description: AccessService.SetAccess (server/internal/service/access.go:181-229) reads the user/request state once via GetUser, then later calls DecideRequest based on that snapshot rather than a fresh read, with no transaction spanning the two. The code's own comment (lines 202-216) already documents the exact race: a request created between the GetUser snapshot and the DecideRequest call can end up permanently stuck in `pending` (if the snapshot said 'no request'), or get resolved with the wrong `decided_by`/status if a new request arrives concurrently with a grant/revoke. The has_access flag itself is written correctly regardless of the race — only request bookkeeping and decided_by attribution are at risk.
findings.impact: Under concurrent access-request submission and admin decision, an access request can be left permanently pending (never resolved by a future CreateRequest, since CreateRequest short-circuits to ErrConflict once access is granted) or get an incorrect decided_by/decided_at audit trail. No effect on the has_access gate itself, so this is a data-integrity/audit gap, not an authorization bypass.
findings.recommendation: Wrap GetUser + SetAccess + DecideRequest in a single database transaction at the repository layer (the code comment already identifies this as the real fix), or re-read the request status immediately before DecideRequest inside the same transaction as the SetAccess write.
findings.cwe: CWE-362: Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization ('Race Condition')

findings.title: RequireSameOrigin's same-origin fallback trusts r.Host, which is only as trustworthy as the reverse proxy in front of it
findings.description: When CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS is empty, RequireSameOrigin (server/internal/handler/middleware.go:203-220) compares the Origin header against `scheme://r.Host` built from the request's own Host header. This is a deliberate, documented tradeoff (Decision 8) and is correctly implemented and tested (TestRequireSameOrigin_Matrix, TestNewMux_ConfigValuesReachMiddleware). Its safety depends entirely on the app container never being reachable except through the nginx reverse proxy that sets `Host: $host` from the validated public request. Verified docker-compose.prod.yml exposes the app container's port via `expose` (internal-only), not `ports` (host-published), which is the correct mitigation — so this is not independently exploitable today. Flagging as defense-in-depth: nothing in the Go code itself enforces that assumption, so a future infra change (e.g. accidentally publishing port 8080, adding a second ingress path, or a misconfigured internal load balancer that forwards an attacker-controlled Host) would silently reopen the CSRF gap this middleware exists to close, with no signal from the application layer.
findings.impact: Currently not exploitable given the reviewed infra config. If the app port is ever exposed directly (bypassing nginx) or an internal proxy forwards a client-controlled Host header, the same-origin fallback becomes bypassable, reopening the login-CSRF and admin-CSRF vectors Decision 8 was written to close.
findings.recommendation: Consider a defense-in-depth layer independent of infra config: either derive the trusted hostname from a required config value (e.g. an explicit PUBLIC_HOST) rather than r.Host when CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS is empty, or add a startup/runtime check that fails closed if the app is reachable on a listener other than the one behind the proxy. Not blocking for this task given the current docker-compose mitigation, but worth tracking.
findings.cwe: CWE-350: Reliance on Reverse DNS/Host Resolution Without Validation

findings.title: normalizePath's admin-login collapse rule matches on relative segment position, not on an actual /api/v1/ prefix check
findings.description: isAdminUserLogin (server/internal/handler/metrics.go:48-50) collapses any path segment that follows two segments literally equal to "admin","users" — it doesn't anchor to /api/v1/. A path such as /foo/admin/users/whatever (which 404s on the real mux, since no such route exists) would still have its third segment collapsed to :id by normalizePath. This is harmless today because WithMetrics only ever sees paths the mux actually dispatches or 404s on, and the label is only used for cardinality control, not for authorization — so it is not exploitable — but it's slightly broader than Decision 18 describes ("третье условие... под /admin/users/") and could mask unrelated future routes' metrics if a path happens to contain that literal sequence.
findings.impact: None security-relevant; purely a metrics-label correctness nit. Included for completeness since Decision 18 was framed as a security fix (Prometheus cardinality DoS via anonymous requests) and this note documents the rule's actual scope versus its stated scope.
findings.recommendation: Optional: anchor the check to i==4 with parts[0..1]=="api","v1" if stricter scoping is desired. Not required — no action needed unless the metrics namespace grows other admin-like paths.

verification_performed.build_and_test: go build ./... clean; go test ./... green across all packages (cmd, internal/auth, internal/config, internal/handler, internal/repository, internal/service) against live MariaDB via TEST_DB_DSN, per the run command supplied in the brief.
bypass_probes_written_and_run: Path-traversal / double-slash / case-folding / missing-trailing-slash / encoded-slash probes against /api/v1/admin/*, /api/v1/users/*, /api/v1/access/* — all either 301-redirected to the canonical path by Go's stdlib ServeMux path cleaning (never reaching handler code un-gated) or fell through to normal 401/404 with the full middleware chain still applied. No bypass found.
Cross-user IDOR probe on /api/v1/users/{userID}/... — CONFIRMED exploitable, see critical finding above.

OPTIONS/CORS preflight interaction with RequireSameOrigin reviewed: OPTIONS is short-circuited by WithCORS before reaching the mux only when CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS is non-empty; when empty, OPTIONS falls through to RequireSameOrigin like any other mutating method and is correctly rejected without an Origin match. No bypass.
verification_performed.hardcoded_secrets_scan: Grepped all Task-5-touched files (access.go, routes.go, metrics.go, config.go, service/access.go, main.go, and their test files) for API_KEY=/SECRET=/PASSWORD=/TOKEN=/private-key patterns. All matches are env-driven config field names/env-var lookups (DBPassword via DB_PASSWORD, YandexClientSecret via YANDEX_CLIENT_SECRET, DeepSeekAPIKey via DEEPSEEK_API_KEY) — no literal credential values in the diff. Confirmed via `git diff` that config.go's only change is the new ContactEmail field/envOrDefault line; the pre-existing DB_PASSWORD dev-default ("poshivon") predates this task and is out of its diff.
verification_performed.owasp_categories_covered: A01 (route-by-route middleware chain audit + IDOR probe — found the critical finding above), A02 (no crypto changed in this task), A03 (JSON decode uses DisallowUnknownFields, no SQL/command construction in reviewed files), A04 (SetAccess race documented as minor finding), A05 (CORS/Origin config reviewed, minor finding on Host-trust), A06 (no new dependencies added, per tech-spec Dependencies section), A07 (session/identity flow traced end-to-end: cookie → DB session lookup → Identity in context, no header-spoofable identity path found), A08 (JSON decoding is strongly-typed Go structs, no deserialization of arbitrary types), A09 (writeAPIDomainError logs every error server-side before responding — verified via TestWriteAPIDomainError_NoInternalTextLeak and TestRequireAuth_UnknownResolverErrorIsNotLeaked), A10 (no server-side outbound requests driven by user input in the reviewed files).
